title: Finite Element-Based Wear Analysis of Automotive Disc Brake Pads Using Archard's Law: A Comparative Study of Friction Lining Materials
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Disc brake performance and service life are strongly influenced by the tribological interaction between the brake pad and rotating rotor. Non-uniform contact pressure, frictional traction, material stiffness, and wear resistance can produce localised material removal and alter the contact state during repeated braking. This paper presents a finite-element-based framework for evaluating pad–rotor contact and predicting progressive wear using a generalised Archard wear formulation. The study is based on a three-dimensional modular brake-corner model described in the supplied project report. A 2.5 kN normal actuation load is considered, and tangential friction is represented through Coulomb friction. Three friction-lining candidates—organic composite, semi-metallic lining, and ceramic matrix composite—are compared using the reported elastic properties, friction coefficients, and dimensional wear coefficients. The source-reported numerical results indicate that inclusion of tangential traction changes the pressure field from a near-symmetric distribution to an asymmetric leading-edge concentration. Under the combined sliding-friction case, the organic baseline reaches approximately 15 µm maximum pad wear after about 2900 rotor revolutions (approximately 2.5 km sliding distance). Across the material cases, reported maximum wear depths are 15.0, 6.2, and 2.1 µm for organic, semi-metallic, and ceramic linings, respectively. title: Whole-Vehicle Brake Wear Emissions Reveal Regenerative-Braking Benefits and Vehicle-Configuration Heterogeneity
abstract: This dataset accompanies the study “Whole-Vehicle Brake Wear Emissions Reveal Regenerative-Braking Benefits and Vehicle-Configuration Heterogeneity.” Brake wear particle emissions were measured from six in-use light-duty vehicles—two battery electric vehicles, two plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, and two internal combustion engine vehicles—using a whole-vehicle wheel-end sampling system on a chassis dynamometer. All vehicles were tested over the complete WLTP-Brake cycle. The four electrified vehicles were each tested under the manufacturer-defined weak and strong regenerative-braking settings. The measurement system was evaluated using brake-disc temperature comparisons, repeated WLTC runs, and CO₂ tracer recovery to assess thermal disturbance, measurement repeatability, and bulk collection performance. The accompanying spreadsheet provides tabulated data associated with the vehicle tests and the analyses reported in the manuscript. These data support comparisons of brake wear emissions between regenerative-braking settings within the same vehicle and among different production vehicle configurations, as well as the examination of particle characteristics and emissions extending beyond deceleration. The six vehicles span different powertrains, vehicle categories, and brake-pad types; they are not intended to provide a statistically representative fleet-average emission factor.

title: Stacking ensemble approach for monitoring the condition of automobile hydraulic brake system
abstract: : This study presents a vibration-based data-driven framework for diagnosing faults in an automobile hydraulic brake system using machine learning and ensemble learning techniques. The dataset comprises 500 vibration signals (50 signals per condition) acquired from a single laboratory-scale brake test rig under ten distinct operating conditions including disc and drum brake pad wear, mechanical fade, reservoir leakage, brake oil spillage, air inclusion in brake fluid, and healthy operation. Autoregressive Moving Average (ARMA) modeling was employed to extract time-domain features followed by feature selection using a J48 decision tree to identify the most significant features. Eight machine learning classifiers namely, logistic model tree (LMT), k-nearest neighbor (kNN), random forest (RF), J48, logistic regression (LR), multilayer perceptron (MLP), support vector machine (SVM) and Naïve Bayes (NB) were evaluated to classify fault conditions and the five best performing ones (LMT, kNN, RF, J48 and NB) were used as base classifiers in the stacking ensemble. To enhance diagnostic robustness, a stacking-based ensemble approach was implemented by combining multiple base classifiers through a meta-classifier. The ensemble models demonstrated consistently improved classification performance compared to individual classifiers. abstract: MY MECHANICS is a car service booking website that brings everything a car owner needs into one place, like an online garage counter. title: Mechanisms governing thermoelastic instability in sliding contact
journal: International Journal of Solids and Structures
abstract: Automotive disc brakes and clutches can develop circumferential hot spots, which can cause vibration, noise and thermal damage. Their onset is commonly described by thermoelastic instability (TEI), driven by a thermomechanical feedback loop. Classical TEI models predict instability thresholds for different geometries and material properties. However, the coupling between thermal and mechanical responses makes it difficult to understand the mechanisms through which these parameters influence stability. These limitations motivate this study, which aims to explain how geometry and material properties govern thermoelastic stability and mode selection. For three canonical sliding-contact configurations of increasing geometric complexity, the characteristic equation is recast as a competition between stabilising thermal diffusion and destabilising thermoelastic feedback. Quantifying these mechanisms shows that geometry and deformation mode primarily affect thermoelastic gain by changing how thermal expansion translates into contact pressure, whereas thermal attenuation depends mainly on perturbation migration and the resulting thermal penetration depth. This decomposition also explains the distinct sensitivities of symmetric and antisymmetric modes to disc and pad material properties. The analysis further shows that the usual dominance of the antisymmetric mode is not universal. title: GCP: A Safety-Aware, Payment-Agnostic Commerce Protocol for Automotive and Mobility Agents
abstract: Personal agents are moving from conversation to commerce. Emerging protocols such as Poppy, UCP, and ACP define how an agent proves whom it represents, discovers merchants, fills a cart, and completes an online checkout. None of them is designed for the commerce that automotive and mobility users actually need: buying a brake pad that fits a specific VIN, booking maintenance at an authorized dealer, binding insurance, or placing a vehicle reservation under safety and consumer-protection rules. This paper proposes GCP 1.0 , an open, capability-based commerce protocol for automotive and mobility agents. GCP adds four things that general commerce protocols lack: (i) vehicle context and safety gates as first-class protocol objects; (ii) a delegation and authorization ladder that lets a human grant bounded purchase authority and revoke it at any time; (iii) a payment-agnostic intent layer that abstracts card, wallet, Alipay, WeChat Pay, OEM finance, and agent-native payment tokens; and (iv) a typed exception and recovery model for the failure modes of real commerce. GCP is compatible by translation: it consumes Poppy identity and session credentials, maps its catalog/cart/checkout objects to UCP and ACP, and carries GCP-specific safety and authorization fields as extension namespaces. title: Explainable machine learning and multi-objective optimization of rubber-based brake friction materials using Krauss test machines through a computational framework
abstract: Rubber-based brake friction materials are evaluated using friction, wear, thermal behavior, and friction stability responses. This study uses, an L27 Taguchi design is performed with respect to five types of rubbers (NR, NBR, SBR, EPDM, and MSR) and three operating factors such as pressure, sliding speed, and interface temperature. Eighty-one experimental data points are obtained based on physical Krauss fade-recovery tests, including three replicates for each design point. Six responses are studied: coefficient of friction, friction stability, fade, recovery, specific wear rate, and maximum interface temperature. A total of 1119 artificial observations were created using the constrained response surface approach, yielding a 1200 data points dataset for the machine learning approach. Comparison of linear regression, random forest, support vector regression, gradient boosting, XGBoost, and ANN methods are done using random and grouped validation. SHAP analysis is performed on the estimated models, while NSGA-II investigates the balance between friction, stability, fade, recovery, wear, and temperature. The 81 observations constitute experimental data, while the remaining 1119 observations are computationally based.

title: Thin-Film Formation of Alq3 and TiO2 by Friction-Transfer Technique Applicable to Organic and Inorganic Materials for Device Applications
journal: Journal of the Society of Materials Science Japan
abstract: Friction-transfer printing has been an excellent technique for achieving thin-film formation of conjugated polymers. In this study, we attempted to fabricate friction-transferred films of small-molecule and inorganic materials that had previously been difficult to transfer. Tris(8-hydroxyquinolinato)aluminum (Alq3) or titanium dioxide (TiO2) powders were mixed with polymeric binders, followed by compression with a hydraulic press to form composite pellets. Friction-transfer printing using the mixed pellets enabled the formation of Alq3 and TiO2 thin films. Notably, the friction-transfer printing process itself operates below 100℃, although a post-annealing treatment at 300℃ can be applied to remove the polymeric binder. As a demonstration of device application, the friction-transferred TiO2 film was successfully implemented in an inverted organic photovoltaic cell. The friction-transfer technique is characterized by low-temperature operation below 100C and extremely short processing times of only a few seconds, suggesting its potential as a novel film-deposition technique for functional materials.

abstract: High-lithium dual-phase Mg–Li alloys exhibit excellent lightweighting potential, but their relatively low strength limits practical applications. title: High-speed laser cladding of Al–TiC composites: How particle architecture governs wear, material retention, and friction behavior
abstract: Euro 7 regulations impose limits on brake wear particle emissions, motivating lightweight low-wear alternatives to cast iron brake disks. This work examines how this architecture influences the tribological response of AlSi7Mg0.6–TiC composites, produced with varying TiC content, laser spot size, and matrix Ti additions, and tested by dry sliding against a silicon nitride ball counterpart. title: Spatial characteristic of temperature distribution and material flow behaviors during bobbin tool friction stir welding: a computational fluid dynamics study
abstract: The incorporation of dual shoulders endows bobbin tool friction stir welding (BT-FSW) with spatially distinct heat transfer and material flow characteristics relative to conventional FSW. The vague understanding of these processes hinders efficient optimization of BT-FSW. To address this gap, a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model, which considered the fully coupling of thermo-mechanical-fluid, was established. The results show that the distribution of contact pressure at the T/W interface constitutes a critical factor governing the temperature field and flow behavior during welding stage. title: Tunable shear thickening in active frictional non-Brownian suspensions
abstract: We study tunable shear thickening in active suspensions of non-Brownian, repulsive, frictional grains using particle-based simulation, finding that activity augments the rheology beyond the friction-mediated shear thickening paradigm. Specifically, up to a crossover activity strength, increasing particle self-propulsion drives a viscosity-reducing 'dethickening' of the system at large stresses, where the material would otherwise be in a thickened, highly viscous state. Above this crossover activity strength, the system enters a thickening regime. Self-propulsion introduces additional isotropic dynamics to the particles, which compete with the flow-driven formation of frictional contacts. The degree of dethickening can thus be tuned by varying a suitably-defined dimensionless active stress that quantifies this competition. Recognising the parallels between self-propulsion and other contemporary routes to dethickening, we demonstrate that our data, within the dethickening regime, are consistent with a recently proposed universal scaling framework, offering a route to tuning the rheology of dense suspensions. Moreover, using the obtained scaling relation, we infer how the shear-jamming and shear-thickening regimes can be tuned by choosing an appropriate self-propulsion strength, and partially validate these inferences with targeted simulations.

title: Frictional instability in dry quartz gouge from room to elevated temperatures
abstract: The frictional properties of fault materials exert a strong influence on fault dynamics and earthquake generation. The velocity dependence of friction, a key factor controlling slip instability, can be modified by temperature, pressure, and the presence of water. Understanding of the frictional properties of dry quartz gouge is necessary to evaluate the effect of water. To investigate the slip stability of dry quartz gouge, velocity-step shear experiments were performed using a double-direct shear apparatus at a normal stress of 10 MPa, temperatures from 30°C to 400°C, and sliding velocities from 0.36 µm/s to 39 µm/s. The steady-state friction coefficients at 3.0 µm/s ranged from 0.619 to 0.712 and showed little temperature dependence. Immediate frictional responses were observed following changes in sliding velocity, and the steady-state friction coefficients decreased with increasing velocity. The velocity-dependent frictional behavior was analyzed within the framework of rate-and-state friction (RSF) theory. The a parameter (direct effect) exhibited a weakly negative or negligible temperature dependence, whereas the b parameter (evolution effect) increased slightly with increasing temperature. As a result, the a – b values were negative at all tested temperatures and became increasingly negative with increasing temperature. These results indicate that frictional instability can occur in dry quartz gouge even in the absence of water.

title: Revealing temperature effects on sliding friction through many-body phonon dynamics
abstract: Despite centuries of research into friction through classical mechanics, the fundamental principles governing friction remain poorly understood, particularly its temperature-dependent nature. This study proposes a quantum theory that reexamines the fundamental principles of tribology. By employing the Feynman diagrammatic perturbation technique within the framework of quantum many-body theory, this study incorporates phonon-phonon interactions to capture the microscopic mechanisms of energy dissipation. The results demonstrate that the phonon radiation governed by harmonic interactions dominates energy dissipation at cryogenic temperatures. As temperature rises, phonon scattering governed by anharmonic interactions overtakes radiation as the primary dissipation mechanism. Further increases in temperature lead to greater damping and suppressed phonon excitation, thereby reducing energy dissipation. The competition among phonon radiation, phonon scattering, and phonon excitation gives rise to the non-monotonic temperature characteristics of friction. Notably, this non-monotonic temperature dependence is also reproduced by classical molecular dynamics simulations. This framework provides a unified understanding of disparate friction trends with temperature observed across different materials, offering insights into the fundamental mechanisms of frictional energy dissipation.

title: Mechanical friction-reduction strategies in triboelectric nanogenerators for enhancing efficiency and durability: A comprehensive review
abstract: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) are a promising technology for harvesting ambient mechanical energy, yet their durability is fundamentally limited by friction-induced wear at functional interfaces. Friction in TENGs is inherently paradoxical: It enables charge generation while simultaneously accelerating material degradation. This review systematically summarizes five advanced mechanical friction-reduction strategies developed to address this paradox, including rolling friction, soft contact, intermittent contact, noncontact, and interface lubrication. Each friction-reduction strategy is systematically evaluated with respect to the corresponding structural design, operating mechanism, and application scenarios in insulator- and semiconductor-based TENGs. Furthermore, a comparative evaluation is conducted to provide a foundational understanding of how friction-reduction methods influence the performance of TENGs and to guide future design optimization. In addition, we outline the emerging trends toward intelligent, integrated triboelectric energy systems and present a roadmap for practical implementation and commercialization. This review offers valuable insights into the path forward for achieving highly efficient and long-term durable TENGs.

title: Additional Influence of the Frictional-Deformation Aspect of Surface Treatment on the Changes in Structure and Properties that Occur in Steels

abstract: The article considers the modern view of the influence of the deformation aspect of processing on the structural state and properties of steels from the point of view of a combination of thermal and mechanical effects that cause significant structural transformations in the surface layers of the material. The main emphasis in the study is placed on considering the influence of the frictional-deformation aspect of processing on changes in the structure and properties of steels during surface strengthening. title: Void Defect Formation Mechanism in Friction Stir Welding of Aluminum Alloys
journal: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
abstract: This thesis establishes a comprehensive framework for understanding defect formation in friction stir welding (FSW) and introduces new quantitative criteria and mechanistic insights for void defects. A systematic and generalizable categorization of FSW defects was developed, enabling consistent interpretation across different materials and joint configurations. Building on this foundation, a detailed review and analysis of defect types observed in various alloys and welding conditions was conducted. Furthermore, void defect formation was investigated through extensive FSW experiments on AA2024, AA5052, and AA7075. A total of 159 bead-on-plate welds were produced with real-time monitoring of temperature, force, and spindle power. Welding parameters spanned travel speeds from 25 to 500 mm/min and tool rotation speeds from 300 to 1500 RPM. Torque thresholds effectively distinguish cavity defects from tunnel and groove defects, while power inputs below approximately 1000 W (AA2024) or 1050 W (AA7075) are generally necessary and sufficient to avoid void defect. title: The Effect of Multi-Pass Friction Stir Processing on Mechanical Properties of Ductile Cast Iron
abstract: Friction stir processing (FSP) is a modification process of friction stir welding (FSW), utilised to modify the surface characteristics of the material. Microstructural recrystallisation and improvements in grain size, structure and mechanical properties are the major achievements of the process. In this study, FSP is employed to improve the microstructure and mechanical properties of ductile cast iron (60-40-18). Analyses and morphological inspections reveal that multiple passes also have a significant impact on the FSPed specimens. An increase in the number of FSP passes leads to a noticeable reduction in the size of intermetallic particles within the stir zone of multi-pass FSP specimens. The improvement in the average grain refinement is 43%. Under the best processing condition for 1, 2 and 3 passes, hardness increased by 37%, 61% and 87%, respectively. The ultimate tensile strength showed slight enhancements of 4.3%, 11% and 21.5%. Wear resistance also improved by 41%, 65% and 75% compared with the base cast iron.

title: Investigation on the anti-friction performance of ink sac-inspired textures under heavy-load conditions
abstract: The working surfaces of PEEK-coated sliding bearings in wind turbines are highly susceptible to severe friction and wear under specific operating conditions of low-speed and heavy-load. To improve the lubrication at the working interface, this paper proposes a novel textured structure inspired by the ink sac structure of cephalopods, adapted to the operating conditions and substrate materials of wind turbines. This new texture utilizes the significant deformation of the PEEK layer to transport lubricant, mimicking the ink-ejection behavior of cephalopods. Samples featuring this novel surface texture were fabricated using 3D printing technology, and a friction and wear test rig was constructed to verify its outstanding anti-friction performance. Under test conditions with the lowest rotational speed and the heaviest load, the coefficient of friction was reduced by 18% compared to that of a smooth specimen. A high-speed camera was used to capture the lubricant delivery process of the new texture under heavy-load conditions. The results demonstrate that the proposed texture exhibits significant oil-squeezing effects; after the system started up in dry-friction state, the coverage of the oily area increased by 63%, and the average grayscale value increased by 18%. Furthermore, the effects of texture shape parameters, texture density, and initial surface oil volume on performance were analyzed. title: Comparison of the Mechanical Behavior of AA5052 and AA6261 Dissimilar Joints by Friction- Stir Welding and Gas Metal Arc Welding
abstract: Welded joints of dissimilar materials offer advantages over those of similar materials in multi-material equipment when combining or alternating different types of raw materials for two-material equipment, plates, and tubes. This is because they allow the characteristics of dissimilar materials to be leveraged for a specific application. For example, a less expensive alloy can be used when fewer properties are required, and a more expensive one for more demanding mechanical or corrosion requirements. Several studies have been conducted on this topic. However, no studies have been published on dissimilar joints of AA5052 and AA6261 using friction stir welding (FSW) and gas metal arc welding (GMAW). This work presents the mechanical properties and microstructural characterization of dissimilar joints of AA5052-H32 and AA6261-T6 obtained by friction stir welding (FSW) and gas metal arc welding (GMAW). Tensile strength, hardness, and microstructure tests were performed to evaluate and compare the mechanical behavior of the samples. Regarding mechanical properties, the FSW joints exhibited greater strength than the GMAW joints.

title: Oil-containing microcapsule-triggered lubrication enables ultralow friction and high wear resistance in phenolic epoxy coatings
abstract: Oil-containing self-lubricating composite material is an effective approach to address the wear issues of polymer materials. In this work, the traditional lubricant 500SN was encapsulated within melamine-formaldehyde (MF) resin shells through in situ polymerization to prepare 500SN@MF microcapsules. Comprehensive characterizations confirmed that the 500SN@MF microcapsules have a well-defined spherical morphology, improved thermal stability, and excellent compatibility with phenolic epoxy resin. The 500SN@MF microcapsules were mixed with phenolic epoxy and cured at room temperature to form a composite self-lubricating coating. Tribological performance tests demonstrated that the composite coating exhibited exceptional anti-wear and friction-reducing properties, with a friction coefficient (COF) of ~0.038 and a notably low wear rate of 0.077×10−6 mm3/(N·m) under a 5 N load and 20,000 friction cycles. Significantly, the 500SN@MF microcapsules could be produced in small batches while maintaining an intact core–shell structure, which offers a scalable material solution for achieving efficient, long-term lubrication in mechanical components and significantly extending their service life.

title: Effect of Chill Modification and Friction Stir Processing on Corrosion Behavior of Zn-0.3Mg Biodegradable Alloy
journal: نشریه علمی پژوهشی مواد پیشرفته در مهندسی
abstract: Introduction and Objectives: Due to the negative impact of increasing Mg content on the ductility and toughness of Zn-Mg alloys, the use of dilute forms of these alloys has recently become more widespread. In this study, the effect of chill modification and friction stir processing (FSP) on the microstructure and corrosion behavior of dilute Zn-0.3Mg alloy were studied. Materials and Methods: The FSP was performed using a simple cylindrical tool under rotation speed of 1600 rpm and travel speed of 12 mm/min on solidified alloy at a cooling rate of 4.1 °C/s. To investigate the effect of chill modification, the solidification rate was increased from 4.1 to 14.7 °C/s. Tafel polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) experiments were performed in simulated body fluid (SBF). title: Production and input use under market frictions: Firm-level evidence for Ethiopia's manufacturing sector
abstract: This paper provides evidence that manufacturing firms in Ethiopia face economically significant constraints in their access to key inputs, particularly raw materials. We show that firms systematically use these inputs less intensively than their marginal contribution to production would warrant, implying the presence of shadow costs, defined as wedges between observed input prices and their true economic value. Our empirical strategy builds on a simple idea: in well-functioning input markets, expenditure shares align with output elasticities. We test this prediction within a production function framework using firm-level panel data for 2003–2016, accounting for input endogeneity. We find strong evidence of misalignment for raw materials, indicating substantial input constraints, while results for energy are less precisely estimated. The findings are robust to an alternative test based on whether lagged inputs predict current input expenditure shares relative to revenue. We also show that more flexible production function specifications can suffer from weak identification, and that simpler models improve statistical power at the cost of stronger structural assumptions. Our results highlight the importance of input market frictions in shaping firm behaviour in Ethiopia.

title: Comparative study of frictional behavior of Cr-doped and Al:Ti-doped DLC coatings on AISI 4140 steel
journal: Journal of Metals Materials and Minerals
abstract: Diamond-like carbon (DLC) coatings have attracted significant interest for applications requiring low friction and high surface durability. Consequently, various DLC formulations have been developed to meet different tribological demands. In this study, the frictional behavior of AISI 4140 carbon steel, which is a widely used high strength structural material, was investigated following surface modification with two distinct DLC coating configurations. Specifically, Cr‒doped DLC with a graded CrCN interlayer (Cr‒DLC/CrCN) and AlTi-doped DLC with a graded AlTiCN interlayer (Al:Ti‒DLC/AlTiCN) were compared. Wear tests were performed using the ball-on-flat method. The results show that the Cr‒DLC/ CrCN coating exhibited a lower coefficient of friction (0.26) than the Al:Ti‒DLC/AlTiCN coating (0.30). Laser scanning confocal microscopy also revealed a smaller wear track on the Cr‒DLC/CrCN surface, with a reduced depth (2.52 µm) and width (496.68 µm). Raman spectroscopy indicated a higher sp2 bonding fraction in the Cr‒DLC/CrCN coating, as reflected by its increased ID/IG ratio, which contributed to its lower friction behavior. Overall, the Cr‒DLC/CrCN coating demonstrated superior tribological performance and wear resistance, making it a more promising surface modification for enhancing the durability of AISI 4140 carbon steel in severe sliding wear environments, typical in oil and gas industries.

title: Polyethylene glycol-based supramolecular gel lubricant with excellent friction-reducing, anti-wear and conductive properties
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to solve the persistent problems of friction, wear and electric erosion faced by bearings, which are critical components in modern machinery. Design/methodology/approach A novel class of supramolecular gel (SG) lubricants was developed using polyethylene glycol 400 (PEG400) and triethylbenzylammonium chloride (TEBAC). A series of SG lubricants with different molar ratios of PEG400 to TEBAC were prepared, and their electrical conductivity and tribological properties were systematically evaluated. Microstructural and worn surface analyses were also conducted. Findings SG1:4 exhibits the optimal tribological performance among the prepared SG lubricants. Compared with commercial grease DG-20E, SG1:4 reduces the friction coefficient by 22.1% and the wear volume by 83.12%. SG1:4 has significantly higher electrical conductivity than DG-20E, which is beneficial for alleviating electric erosion. The excellent performance of SG1:4 is attributed to its unique structure and the in situ formed tribochemical reaction film on the friction surface. Originality/value This work proposes a new type of SG lubricant with outstanding tribological properties and high electrical conductivity, providing a novel strategy for the development of high-performance anti-electric erosion lubricating materials for bearings. title: Mechanical and metallurgical characterization of ZE41 magnesium alloy joints produced by indirect cooled friction stir welding
abstract: Conventional friction stir welding of ZE41 magnesium alloy presents challenges related to nonuniform heat distribution, weld thinning, and microstructural deterioration, which can compromise joint integrity and mechanical performance. To overcome these limitations, the present study employs indirect cooling-assisted friction stir welding (ICFSW) using a specially designed hybrid fixture to regulate heat dissipation and improve weld quality. An underground tank was fabricated and fastened to the fixture plate. Three distinct cooling media were used in the cooling tank. We tested the mechanical and metallurgical properties of the welded specimens. With the process parameters fine-tuned, the tensile test results were obtained. Tank coolant reaches its ultimate tensile strength at 400 rpm. The heat-affected zone was tested microstructurally. One of the main problems, especially in indirect-cooled friction stir welding, is that it thins out the weld and causes premature loss of material plasticity. Wrinkles and thermal quenching were reduced due to the storage tank’s consistent heating and cooling while welding. Different cooling media produced distinct microstructural characteristics in the ICFSW joints, as observed through SEM analysis. To distinguish between different microstructural zones and to measure the welded region’s hardness, microhardness was measured, which may contribute to sustainable industrialisation.

title: Mechanistic Insights into Coupled Pin Shoulder Eccentricity for Controlling Defect Formation and Microstructural Evolution in Friction Stir Welding
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
abstract: Tool runout and eccentricity are identified as crucial yet under-explored issues impacting thermomechanical fields and weld integrity in friction stir welding. Although pin offsets have been studied in the past, the simultaneous action of pin and shoulder eccentricities on defect formation, asymmetry in material flow, and microstructural evolution is poorly understood. This study presents a systematic investigation of these coupled eccentricities and they control the weld quality. Experiments indicate that increasing pin eccentricity alone intensifies local strain and heat generation, promoting unsteady material flow leading to wormhole defects and, at higher magnitudes, externally visible surface grooves. Conversely, when both pin and shoulder are offset by equal amounts, the resulting synchronized runout stabilizes material flow, fully eliminating defect initiation and producing a sound weld zone despite identical eccentricities. Microstructural evaluation, interpreted through the Zener–Hollomon parameter, exhibits distinct strain rate and temperature histories associated with each eccentricity condition, leading to measurable differences in dynamic recrystallization behavior and grain refinement. Cyclic thermal variations are caused by the eccentric tool, owing to oscillatory frictional and plastic dissipation modifying the precipitation kinetics in heat-treatable Aluminum alloys. title: Tribological Performance and Interfacial Interaction Mechanisms of Micro‐Arc Oxidation Modified Friction Pairs Under Wide‐Temperature Conditions
abstract: To investigate the tribological behavior and failure mechanisms of micro‐arc oxidation‐modified friction pairs over a wide temperature range, two graphene oxide (GO) modified friction pair systems, T1 (Al 2 O 3 /GO‐PTFE/CuO) and T2 (Al 2 O 3 /GO‐PI/CuO), were evaluated at 30, 60, 90, 120, and 150 °C. T1 exhibited lower coefficients of friction (COFs) and wear rates below 90 °C, but both increased sharply above 90 °C due to thermally induced softening of polytetrafluoroethylene, molecular chain agglomeration, and transfer film degradation. From 30 to 150 °C, the COF and wear rate of T1 increased by ≈204.6% and 656%, respectively. In contrast, owing to the superior thermal stability of polyimide, T2 exhibited more gradual increases in COF and wear rate, by ≈151.2% and 391%, respectively. Worn surface observations indicated that thermal softening induced material agglomeration and transfer film instability dominated the wear of T1, whereas progressively intensified abrasive wear dominated T2. These results demonstrate distinct temperature‐dependent tribological behaviors and provide guidance for temperature‐adaptive selection of friction pair materials.

title: Frictional Controls on Shallow Megathrust Slip: Field and Experimental Constraints from the Chugach-Kodiak Accretionary Wedge, Alaska
abstract: Subduction megathrusts accommodate a range of slip behaviors, from earthquakes to slow slip events and stable creep, but the controls governing their distribution remain poorly constrained. We investigate hydromechanical and lithologic controls on frictional behavior in the Mesozoic McHugh Complex (Alaska), an exhumed accretionary complex representative of the shallow plate interface (prehnite-pumpellyite facies). We integrate field observations with compositional and microstructural analyses and laboratory friction experiments on representative fault gouges and host rocks. Structural observations reveal that the accretionary complex incorporated inherited heterogeneity from the incoming plate. Experiments conducted under air-dry and water-saturated conditions at room temperature and normal stresses of 10–40 MPa show that frictional behavior is strongly controlled by composition. Water saturation preferentiallyweakens phyllosilicate-rich materials, promoting velocity-strengthening behavior. Organicrich argillitic gouges exhibit the lowest friction coefficients ( µ f ≈ 0.33) and accommodated stable creep, consistent with field evidence for strain concentration in these rocks. Cherts and veined pillow basalts are stronger ( µ f ≈ 0.53) and exhibit velocity-weakening tendencies. Basalt-hosted fault zones with chlorite-enrichment show transitional, near velocity-neutral behavior. Our results indicate that stable, unstable, and conditionally stable slip coexisted along the shallow

title: Hard domain–soft domain interaction facilitating LCF failure in friction stir welding joints with macroscopic heterogeneity
abstract: Aluminum alloys friction stir welding joints are macroscopically heterogeneous due to inherently softened heat affected zone (HAZ), which will generate hard domain–soft domain interaction under cyclic loading. By combining precipitates’ characterization with macroscopic digital image correlation, this work found that deformation incompatibility between soft HAZ and neighboring hard domains drives pronounced cyclic plastic strain localization in HAZ, triggering crack initiation. This incompatibility simultaneously generates back stress and induces a compressive ratcheting effect via Bauschinger effect, generating fatigue-ratcheting synergistic damage to expedite failure. These findings elucidate how hard domain–soft domain interaction accelerates fatigue failure of heterogeneous joints, with implications for other heterostructure materials. IMPACT STATEMENT We applied digital image correlation to uncover the hard–soft domain interaction inducing cyclic strain localization and fatigue-ratcheting synergistic damage mechanisms in fatigue behaviors of friction stir welding joints.

title: Effect of cooling conditions on microstructure evolution and tensile deformation behavior of friction stir welded NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy
abstract: The influence of cooling conditions on the microstructure and transverse tensile behavior of friction stir welded NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy was investigated by comparing air-cooled friction stir welding (AFSW) with alcohol–dry ice-assisted friction stir welding (LFSW) under identical nominal welding parameters. Both conditions produced sound joints containing fine, predominantly equiaxed grains in the nugget zone (NZ). Compared with AFSW, LFSW reduced the average grain size from 4.85 to 3.75 µm in the upper NZ and from 4.77 to 3.93 µm in the lower NZ. The finer-grained LFSW joint exhibited a higher yield strength (546 ± 3 MPa) than AFSW (471 ± 3 MPa), while their ultimate tensile strengths remained comparable (828 ± 7 and 836 ± 4 MPa, respectively). In contrast, uniform elongation decreased from 62.9 ± 5% for AFSW to 25.0 ± 2% for LFSW. Electron backscatter diffraction revealed progressive grain subdivision and recrystallization across the base material–thermo-mechanically affected zone–NZ transition in both joints. Digital image correlation further showed that plastic strain was preferentially accommodated outside the refined NZ, with more pronounced spatial strain partitioning in the LFSW joint. These results demonstrate that intensified external cooling promotes NZ grain refinement and increases joint yield strength, but its benefit is offset by reduced deformation compatibility during transverse tension. title: Evaluation of the mechanical behavior of aluminum/aluminum foam/aluminum sandwich panels fabricated by Bobbin Tool Friction Stir Welding
abstract: Aluminum Foam Sandwich (AFS) panels are extensively used in rail transportation, aerospace, and military applications because of their lightweight design, high specific strength and stiffness, and impact resistance. This study investigates the mechanical behavior of aluminum foam-to-aluminum sheet joints fabricated using Bobbin Tool Friction Stir Welding (BT-FSW). Based on the tested welding conditions, a traverse speed of 12 mm/min and a rotational speed of 1250 rpm were selected for joint fabrication. The mechanical properties of the welded panels were evaluated through compression, three-point bending, and interfacial shear tests. The welded sample exhibited a maximum compressive stress of 99.1 MPa at a compressive strain of 0.3135, a maximum load of 7250.8 N in three-point bending, and a maximum load of 2104 N in the interfacial shear test. These results demonstrate the feasibility of achieving direct bonding between the face sheets and the foam core through friction stir welding, without the need for additional adhesives or brazing materials. The findings highlight the potential of BT-FSW as a joining technique for aluminum foam sandwich panels, based on the mechanical responses obtained from the conducted tests.

title: Three-Dimensional Thermomechanical Analysis of Radial Friction Welding of Dissimilar Copper-Aluminum Alloys: Finite Element Modelling and Experimental Validation
abstract: This study investigates radial friction welding of dissimilar AA2024 aluminum and Cu-DHP copper using a three-dimensional finite element model together with optical metallography, Vickers microhardness measurements, and thermocouple measurements. A coupled thermomechanical model was implemented in ANSYS Workbench 2023 R1 at 1 400 rpm and 30 MPa. The numerical solution predicts an asymmetric thermal field with a maximum of 750 °C at the Al-Cu interface, an equivalent plastic strain of 0.0177 mm/mm, and a maximum total displacement of 0.130 mm. The strain and displacement fields were interpreted together with the optical observations, which indicate localized thermomechanical modification and preferential material flow near the interface. The thermomechanically affected zone (TMAZ) reached approximately 157 HV. Direct comparison with thermocouple measurements and the measured aluminum-side TMAZ width supported the model for the directly comparable quantities. Microhardness provides complementary evidence of localized hardening but does not constitute direct strain measurement or phase identification. The model is useful for interpreting the thermomechanical response of AA2024/Cu-DHP radial friction welds, while the assumptions regarding friction and radiation, the absence of latent heat, and the absence of microstructural-kinetics modelling remain explicit limitations.

title: Multi-criteria evaluation of tool pin geometry in friction stir welding of dissimilar aluminium alloy using Grey Relational analysis
abstract: Joint performance in friction stir welding is strongly influenced by tool pin geometry, as changes in pin profile can modify material flow and the associated thermal–mechanical conditions around the tool. This study investigates three pin geometries: cylindrical, tapered, and stepped, for joining the dissimilar aluminium alloys AA6061-T6 and AA5052-H32, with every weld produced under identical process settings so that any change in outcome could be attributed solely to pin design. Joint quality was assessed through tensile testing, Vickers hardness mapping, and optical microscopy of the stir zone, with particular attention to how grain structure in this region relates to the measured mechanical properties. To rank the three geometries on a single scale, the individual performance responses were combined into a composite index using Grey Relational Analysis (GRA), enabling identification of the pin design that gives the best overall joint performance.

title: Thermo-Mechanical Material Screening and Constraint-Based Optimization of an Automotive Clutch Using Response Surface Methodology
abstract: This study presents an integrated computational framework combining multiscale material homogenization, transient thermo-mechanical analysis, and constraint-based optimization for automotive clutch design. Using ANSYS Material Designer, polymer matrix composites containing 15 vol.% Al₂O₃ were initially evaluated against a commercial friction material (COM_FM). Preliminary finite element analysis (FEA) indicated that increased thermal conductivity alone was insufficient to limit localized temperature rise. A composite containing 25 vol.% Al₂O₃ (PMC-M1-25) was therefore selected for further investigation. A 30-point design space was constructed using Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) with an optimal space-filling (OSF) configuration, considering clamping pressure (1.0–3.0 MPa), engine torque (150–350 N.m), and friction coefficient (0.25–0.40). Response surface methodology (RSM) was used to model global component deformation and peak interface temperature. The maximum sampled temperature reached 456.83°C, highlighting the importance of evaluating thermally unfavorable operating conditions. Sensitivity analysis and response surface models were used to examine the effects of the operating parameters on the thermo-mechanical responses. Constraint-based optimization was then applied to identify operating conditions satisfying the prescribed thermal limit, followed by direct FEA verification of the selected condition. title: Intuitionistic Fuzzy Multi‐Criteria decision process parameter Optimization Model for Friction Stir Welding Parameters for Dissimilar Directionally rolled ETP Copper and AA6063 Alloy
abstract: This work addresses the optimization of Friction Stir Welding (FSW) parameters for dissimilar directionally rolled Electrolytic Tough Pitch (ETP) copper and AA6063 aluminum alloy by hybrid approach of Response Surface Methodology (RSM) and Integrated Fuzzy Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (IFMCDA). The influence of tool rotational speed, traverse speed, tilt angle and tool profile on the welding performance is investigated using a -optimal experimental design in the RSM framework. A quadratic regression model is developed to establish the relations between the process parameters and response variables. The optimization has been carried out taking into account multi-performance properties such as ultimate tensile strength (UTS), elongation, microhardness (HV0.5) and corrosion resistance. Then the IFMCDA is used to solve the multi-objective optimization problem by integrating fuzzy logic and multi-criteria decision making, which can choose the best welding parameters under conflicting performance requirements. Sensitivity analysis and confirmation experiments are performed to assess the robustness and predictive accuracy of the proposed models. The study highlights the complementary roles of RSM in process modelling and IFMCDA in multi-objective decision making. The integrated methodology proposed here provides a reliable framework for optimizing the FSW process parameters and improving the weld quality of dissimilar material joints. The study is limited to AA6063 alloy and ETP

title: Influence of Tib2 Reinforcement and Tool Traverse Speed on the Structural and Thermal Behavior of Dissimilar Metals (AA7075–AA2024) of Friction Stir Welded Joints: an ABAQUS Study
journal: i-manager s Journal on Material Science
abstract: Friction Stir Welding (FSW) is a modern solid-state joining technique known for its energy efficiency, strong joints, and minimal environmental impact. This project focuses on joining two dissimilar high-strength aluminium alloys AA7075 and AA2024 using the simulation software ABAQUS. The welding was performed on the plates measuring 200 mm in length, 60 mm in width, and 6 mm in thickness. In this study, a Finite Element (FE) simulation was performed to understand the structural and thermal behaviour during welding. Various process parameters were tested, including tool rotational speed, feed rate and tilt angle to identify the most effective settings for achieving strong and defect-free joints. The simulation showed that the welding parameters were Tool speeds of 1000,2000 and 3000 rpm; Feed rates of 1,2 and 3 mm/sec; Tilt angles of 10,1.50 and 2°. These parameters produced in a moderate peak temperature of approximately 580°C, which is within the ideal plasticization range for both AA7075 and AA2024 without exceeding their melting points. This ensures proper material flow, defect-free weld formation, and maintenance of the mechanical properties.

title: Hybrid machine learning framework for the classification and prediction of dry sliding wear performance of friction stir processed and laser shock peened AA6061-O alloy
abstract: This study presents a hybrid machine learning model (classification and regression) based framework to understand the tribological properties of Aluminium alloy 6061 (AA6061). At first hybrid experimental approach combining friction stir processing (FSP) and laser shock peening (LSP) was conducted with the AA6061-O alloy (base material). For this, wear rate (W R ) of AA6061 is observed as a function of variable applied load (AL - 10, 20, and 30 N), variable sliding velocity (SV - 1, 2, and 3 m/s) and constant sliding distance (SD – 1000 m). Analysis of variance (ANOVA) showed that AL and SV significantly influenced W R (p < 0.05), contributing more than 89% to the total variation. Results obtained from the real-time experiments are then used to train, test and validate both machine learning (ML) models. Results recorded by the J48 decision tree proven its balanced classifying ability across both HIGH and LOW classes. The weighted average F-measure of 0.892 for BM, 0.886 for FSP, and 0.886 for LSP. Meanwhile, results recorded by the extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) validated its combined gradient boosting nature with regularization and effective handling of nonlinear relationships, and strong generalization. Also, this study attempts the generalization of the proposed model through the model interpretability study. title: Influence of gas flow parameters on the velocity of bulk materials
journal: Kompleksnoe Ispolzovanie Mineralnogo Syra = Complex Use of Mineral Resources
publisher: "Institute of Metallurgy and Ore Beneficiation" JSC
abstract: This article examines the flow patterns and kinetics of granular media interacting with ascending and descending gas flows. Bulk material release control is a critical aspect of shaft furnace and hopper operation Experimental studies were conducted on a flat transparent model and a close-up "hot" model using high-speed video recording (SK-16). With an error in the calculated values of the critical speed, amounting from to -30.0 to +28.8 , the main parameters varied within the following limits: specific gravity and viscosity of the gas, respectively, from 11.97 to 1.16 N/m3; from ; diameter, specific gravity and coefficient of internal friction of bulk material from m; from kN/m3; from ; coefficient taking into account the shape of the particles, from ; outlet diameter from m; attitude equals . The materials studied were agglomerate, lime, millet, and coke; the gas phases were air, helium, and hydrogen. It was established that the outflow mechanism is staged and determined by the frequency of destruction of dynamically unstable vaults. It was found that gas density is the key factor influencing the outflow rate, while the effect of viscosity is secondary. An analytical relationship was formulated for calculating the critical gas velocity that causes layer suspension. abstract: Companion Supplemental Materials for the manuscript "Unified Energetics-Based Model for Bedload Transport on Steep Slopes and Mixed-Size Beds" (submitted to Journal of Hydraulic Engineering, ASCE). title: Design and Analysis of Scientific Networks on the Emerging and Safe Explosive Material (TKX-50) Using the Scientometric Software VOSviewer
abstract: One of the fundamental principles of passive defense is the reduction of vulnerability of critical and military facilities against enemy attacks through non-armed strategies. Safe explosives, by mitigating unintended risks (such as accidental detonations or sabotage), contribute to enhancing the safety and security of infrastructures. The simultaneous increase in explosive power and reduction in sensitivity has led to the development of new generations of energetic materials. Among the noteworthy compounds in this context is dihydroxylammonium 5,5′-bis(tetrazolate)-1,1′-diolate (TKX-50). The primary objective of the present study is to design scientific networks of safe and emerging explosives (TKX-50) using the VOSviewer software. The methodology involves employing VOSviewer to analyze data retrieved from Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus databases. The project is structured into seven stages: monitoring organization, search and collection cycle, analysis and meta-analysis, image updating, trend analysis and estimation, validation, and dissemination with feedback. Findings indicate that emerging explosives, as safer materials with reduced environmental impact and higher explosive performance, can serve as alternatives to currently utilized energetic compounds in applied industries. title: A Compression–Shear-Enhanced Nonlocal Macro–Meso-Scale Consistent Damage Model Considering Residual Shear Strength for Quasi-Brittle Materials
abstract: The compression–shear fracture of quasi-brittle materials involves crack closure, frictional sliding and residual shear resistance, whereas the original nonlocal macro–meso-scale consistent damage (NMMD) model cannot capture compression–shear and mixed tension/compression–shear failure. This paper proposes an improved NMMD model for compression–shear-dominated fracture. Potential shear failure planes are determined using the Mohr–Coulomb criterion. Material-point-pair relative displacements are projected onto these planes to construct a nonlocal shear strain measure and a compression stress-dependent critical shear damage threshold. A shear topological damage variable is defined via the history-dependent maximum overshoot, and a pressure-sensitive energy degradation function is formulated for the residual shear strength. The total strain energy density is decomposed into tensile, compressive–volumetric and compressive–deviatoric components. Separate energy degradation mechanisms for tension and compression–shear damage establish the mixed-mode fracture constitutive relation. Implemented within an explicit finite element framework, the model is validated by direct shear and uniaxial compression benchmark simulations of pre-flawed specimens. title: Why Ice Is So Slippery
abstract: We simulate nanoscale ice-glass friction from first principles and upscale it by modeling frictional heating. Nanoscale simulations alone overestimate friction and miss its velocity dependence. Frictional heating warms the contact toward the melting point, thickening the premelting film tenfold and cutting its viscosity a hundredfold; friction drops with velocity, matching experiment. Premelting forms the film without sliding or heating, but its slipperiness hinges on frictional heating, as Bowden and Hughes proposed in 1939, without melting. Snow, other materials, and coatings remain open.

title: Realistic large-scale three-dimensional particle modelling of stockpile formation and reclaim with insights into ore mixing and segregation
abstract: Stockpiles serve as critical elements for grade management, blending, and surge control in mining operations. They are integral across various stages of mining, from extraction at the mine site to transportation at the port. One common method for depleting stockpiles is through the utilisation of gravity reclaim systems, which involve hoppers integrated with conveyors positioned beneath the stockpile. However, despite their widespread adoption, stockpiles with gravity reclaim systems can create mixing, segregation and suboptimal discharge flow due to design limitations of the hoppers and the characteristics of the materials being handled. The flow of granular material during discharge is heavily influenced by factors such as internal cohesion, which can be affected by parameters like moisture content, particle size and shape distribution, particularly with materials containing high fine and clay content. This study employs very large-scale numerical simulation through the Discrete Element Method (DEM) to analyse a conical coarse ore stockpile with a range of discharge configurations. DEM, although computationally intensive, offers deep insight into the flow dynamics of cohesive and frictional materials during discharge, at both micro and macro scales. The focus is on informing the development of more efficient mineral process models to manage variable ore quality. The large scale, detailed, DEM modelling enables quantification of segregation and mixing that may occur during b

title: Finite Element Analysis of Contact Characteristics of Soluble Pigs in DN100 Gas-Gathering Pipelines
abstract: Nonlinear contact finite element models of foam-shaped and spherical soluble pigs in a DN100 gas-gathering pipeline were established using common two-parameter Mooney–Rivlin material parameters and pipe dimensions. Displacement-controlled analyses examined the effects of interference and friction on contact pressure distributions, while local contact region changes during weld passage were discussed. Pressure-driven analyses determined numerical start-up pressure differences using a prescribed contact status criterion. Within the investigated conditions, increasing interference raised the contact pressures for both geometries. Increasing friction altered axial pressure distributions and reversed the ranking of the mean contact pressure. The numerical start-up pressure differences increased with interference and friction and were higher for the foam-shaped pig under the investigated nonzero-friction conditions. Contact pressure levels, load distributions, and the driving requirement for reaching the prescribed sliding state should therefore be considered together. These comparisons apply to the adopted material description, loading procedures, and initial undissolved state; quantitative engineering application requires further validation.

title: Tribological model of concrete fracture resistance during compression
abstract: The article considers a tribological model of concrete's resistance to fracture during compression. The mechanism of concrete destruction, the structure of which is multiscale and invariant, is still described by classical methods of deformable solid mechanics. This does not take into account that the concrete structure is heterogeneous, coarse-heterogeneous, multiphase, and contains various types of defects. Destruction is considered as an instantaneous act that occurs under a certain limiting condition. Computational models are constructed without taking into account the heterogeneity and multiscale structure of the material. The authors of the article propose to consider the destruction of concrete as a process in the development of which the forces of internal friction play an important role. The dependences of concrete strength on the coefficient of internal friction are presented, and a mechanomolecular model for calculating the coefficient of internal friction is proposed.

title: Semi-Implicit Pairwise Descent for Nonlocal Continuum Mechanics
abstract: We propose Semi-Implicit Pairwise Descent (SIPD), a unified nonlocal pairwise framework for simulating large-scale hyperelastic materials involving complex contact and friction. By reformulating the Finite Element Method (FEM) equations of motion into a pairwise force representation from a nonlocal perspective, our approach avoids costly Hessian computations, leading to a reduction in per-iteration computational overhead. Furthermore, we propose an analytical projection strategy for projecting our Hessian-free coefficient matrices to positive semi-definiteness. And we treat contact and friction as a unified anisotropic elastic energy, allowing for a seamless integration into the elastic solver framework. We mathematically prove that our method is unconditionally stable and numerically convergent. Experimental results demonstrate that SIPD achieves real-time performance for million-scale simulations even under intricate contact and friction conditions.

title: Model-free stiffness measurement of microscale soft contacts by far-field traction force microscopy
abstract: The microscale stiffness of soft materials governs their contact mechanics, adhesion and friction, yet it is surprisingly difficult to measure. Micro or nanoindentation is typically used, but extracting stiffness from these measurements requires using contact mechanics models (e.g. JKR), whose assumptions often break down for soft adhesive contacts. Here, we introduce far-field traction force microscopy (FF-TFM) to extract stiffness without using any contact model. We drag a colloidal probe mounted on an atomic-force microscope across a soft surface, measuring the friction force while imaging the displacements of fluorescent tracers on the substrate. Far from the contact, in the elastic limit, these lateral displacements depend solely on the friction force and the substrate stiffness, and fitting them with the point-force solution thus gives the substrate's Young's modulus directly. We successfully match bulk rheology moduli with FF-TFM for six different silicone elastomers, where JKR fits to indentation data underestimate moduli by as much as 40\% of their bulk values. Our approach also enables tracking how the probe slips across the surface. We find that soft contacts can "pre-slip" with no detectable signature in the force signal, unlike stiffer contacts. FF-TFM thus offers a contact-model-free route to measuring microscale stiffness and slip behavior in soft materials.

title: Determination of Antifriction Properties of Alloys of Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Groups during Wear Tests after Applying Different Approaches to Modifying their Surfaces
abstract: The study is devoted to determining the antifriction properties of iron-based alloys and aluminum-based alloys in wear tests after applying different approaches to modifying their surfaces. The results of modifying the surface of 65G steel samples using the additional friction-deformation strengthening (AFDS) method and D16 aluminum alloy samples using the microarc oxidation (MAO) method are considered. It is shown that the combination of thermal and mechanical or physical and chemical effects initiates significant structural changes in the surface and near-surface layers of the material. Studies of surface quality, results of macro-, microscopic analysis, durometric and other types of studies explain the relationship between the evolution of the microstructure and the change in properties in the zone of friction-strain and physico-chemical effects on the surface. The antifriction characteristics of the sample surfaces after exposure to the above methods were investigated using the SMC-2 friction machine according to the “disk-pad” scheme. title: Institutional Reality as a Correctible Evidence Chain
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Institutional systems may preserve records of claims without preserving what was knowable when those claims were made, who was authorized to act, whether execution actually occurred, or what subsequent external evidence established. This methodological working paper introduces Institutional Reality as a Correctible Evidence Chain, a provenance-oriented reporting framework developed by the System Friction Institute. The method distinguishes observations, source evidence, inferences, authorization, execution, externally observed consequences, and subsequent corrections while preserving temporal integrity and institutional accountability. The paper defines a structured evidence-chain model, a compact Reality Passport, and four falsifiable hypotheses for future independent evaluation against conventional documentation, provenance, and audit workflows. Bounded institutional continuity observations and public documentary material illustrate the feasibility of maintaining explicit distinctions between identity, state, evidence, and authority. Research status: The manuscript presents a methodological specification and documentary illustrations, not an independently validated empirical finding. No independent comparative superiority, general predictive validity, or external scientific replication is claimed. Publication classification: Institutional working paper; not peer reviewed. title: A coupled phase-field finite-element model to simulate hotspot dynamics of energetic composites
journal: Modelling and Simulation in Materials Science and Engineering
abstract: Understanding accidental ignition of energetic composites essentially requires microstructure -sensitive models that efficiently predict hotspot dynamics at the micro-scale for ignition initiation. 1) This work introduces a computational framework that uses Finite Element Method coupled with Phase Field analysis. This model is implemented in Abaqus/Explicit for simulating hotspot dynamics of polymer-bonded explosives (PBXs) subjected to low-velocity impacts (130–190 m/s). The framework couples the mechanical deformation and thermal heating using user-defined subroutines (VUMAT for elastic behavior and frictional heating and VUMATHT via a thermal analogy for the phase-field fracture). Frictional heat generation is modelled using a phenomenological contact-based formulation. 2) A hybrid strain energy decomposition scheme is further proposed that degrades only the tensile deviatoric contribution.The hybrid scheme is motivated by the mixed-mode shear–compressive fracture at grain–binder interfaces, and is supported indirectly by a rock-mechanics benchmark. The coupled computational framework effectively captures localized hotspot formation driven primarily by frictional heating, emphasizing the significant influence of particle morphology and binder–particle interfaces on the ignition initiation. This approach offers an efficient alternative to discrete cohesive finite element-based frameworks for simulating accidental ignition of energetic materials.

title: Quantitative Analysis and Mechanistic Insights on the Nanoscratch Characteristics of CoCrNi Medium Entropy Alloy
abstract: The CoCrNi medium entropy alloy (MEA) has received attention lately owing to its remarkable mechanical properties and peculiar deformation mechanisms. In the present study, nanoscratch tests were conducted to investigate the role of crystallographic orientation on friction, wear volume, and associated deformation mechanism of single-crystalline equiatomic CoCrNi MEA using experiments and 3D molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The nanoscratch tests using MD simulations were conducted on (100) [001], (111) [110], and (110) [110] cases. The experimentally observed plastically deformed material, characterized by pileup accumulation during nanoscratch, was qualitatively consistent with the profile of pileup obtained from simulations. Chemical inhomogeneity and lattice distortion ensured a uniform and stable dislocation field during nanoscratch, leading to symmetric pileup in all the cases. The close values of average lengths of sessile dislocations caused similar strain hardening that led to close values of coefficients of friction and a narrow range of wear volumes across different crystallographic orientations. Results showed that CoCrNi MEA has significantly low anisotropy for the nanoscratch properties of the material. Low stacking fault energy indicated the formation of nanotwins and phase transformation along with planar slip as the dominant mechanism during nanoscratch. title: Study on the Multi‐Environment Anti‐Aging Performance of Nano‐Textured PTFE – Al 2 O 3 Hybrid FKM Composites
abstract: Fluoroelastomer (FKM) is widely used in aerospace sealing but suffers from synergistic degradation caused by thermal oxidative aging, low temperature embrittlement, salt spray corrosion, and oil swelling. In this study, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) and aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3 ) hybrid nanofillers were incorporated into the FKM matrix and surface, and tailored microstructures were engineered to fabricate a FKM/PTFE/Al 2 O 3 composite. The composite exhibited excellent stability under harsh conditions: after exposure to 200°C and −20°C, and after immersion in 5 wt% NaCl solution and hydraulic oil, its hardness change remained within ±3%, outperforming pristine FKM. Tribological tests showed friction coefficient reductions of 61.3% at high temperature, 68.2% at low temperature, 62.5% after NaCl solution immersion and 80.5% after hydraulic oil immersion compared to aged FKM, along with significantly reduced wear depth. PTFE provides self‐lubrication that minimizes adhesion and friction, while well‐dispersed Al 2 O 3 nanoparticles act as physical barriers to inhibit medium penetration, reinforce the matrix, and suppress crack initiation and propagation. A multiscale mechanism involving structure guidance, material response, and interface self‐repair underpins these improvements, greatly enhancing FKM's anti‐aging and wear resistance in extreme environments and offering a promising route for high performance sealing materials.

title: Comprehensive review on thermo‐hydraulic performance enhancement of solar air collector
abstract: Solar air collector is commonly used for low‐ and medium‐temperature applications like space heating, drying, and various industrial processes, particularly because of their simple design and low operating cost. In this paper, a comprehensive review is made on the novel techniques used to improve the performance of the solar air collector. The performance of the various techniques is examined by numerous heat transfer parameters like Nusselt number enhancement ratio, friction enhancement ratio, thermal efficiency and thermal enhancement ratio. The implementation of artificial roughness in the form of ribs, baffles, fins protrusion, cavities and vortex generators strongly improves the heat transfer and significantly enhances the thermal performance of SAC through strong turbulence and well mixing. For hemispherical cavity rib‐turbulators, a maximum Nusselt number enhancement ratio of 5.33 is achieved within the range of parameters considered. Solar air collector with phase change materials strengthens thermal energy storage, outlet temperature stability and operational time with an enhancement in thermal efficiency of 5%–17% in this study. Jet impingement with multi‐arc ribs under optimized conditions is concluded as the case that provides a maximum thermal enhancement ratio of 4.1 within the designed parameters. title: Tribological Performance and Interfacial Lubrication Mechanism of PTFE/PEEK Composites Modified with PMPS@PSF Microcapsules
abstract: Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)-based composites are promising self-lubricating materials, yet pure PTFE suffers from poor wear resistance and unstable transfer films. Here, polymethylphenylsiloxane@polysulfone (PMPS@PSF) core–shell microcapsules were prepared by solvent evaporation and incorporated with polyetheretherketone (PEEK) into PTFE. The effects of composition, load, and rotational speed on tribological performance were systematically evaluated. Increasing PEEK content markedly reduced wear but slightly increased friction. The composite containing 30 wt % PEEK and 10 wt % PMPS@PSF exhibited the best overall performance, with a COF of 0.0462 and a wear-loss rate of 0.0185 g/h at 30 N and 300 rpm, representing reductions of 57.30% and 90.28%, respectively, compared with pure PTFE. Mechanistic analysis and worn-surface characterization support a proposed bilayer lubrication mechanism involving PTFE-rich fluorinated species and PMPS-derived components, whose synergistic lubrication contributes to improved friction reduction and wear resistance.

title: Exploratory Fuzzy Decision Support for Tribological Screening of Carbon and Glass Fiber Composites for Potential External Prosthesis Covers
journal: International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems
abstract: Composite selection requires a transparent treatment of competing wear, friction, and thermal responses. This study examines fifteen tabulated tribological records for carbon and carbon/glass epoxy configurations and the mathematical requirements of a spherical fuzzy decision framework relevant to external prosthesis covers. Hand lay-up and ambient-temperature curing define the fabrication route. The records cover nominal loads of 400–800 N, rotational speeds of 2–6 rev/min, and sliding distances of 20–60 m. The wear response spans 0.088–0.206 mm/h and mass loss spans 2.058–3.528 mg. At 400 N and 20 m, the GG-coded record had a 16.95% lower wear response than the CC-coded record at 6 rev/min and twice the CC value at 2 rev/min. Displayed fuzzy entries are examined, and triangular ratings are recalculated from their stated counts. A separate equal-weight VIKOR baseline uses the six numerical responses. Record 7 ranks first across five compromise settings and twelve individual weight perturbations, and after excluding both friction-related columns; at v = 1, records 7 and 3 form the compromise set. The load–friction inconsistency, incomplete criterion mapping, and rank deficiency of the specified response-surface design limit interpretation. The results support conditional screening of records under stated decision assumptions, rather than a validated material optimum, measured tensile or adhesive strengths, predictive model validity, or prosthetic-component qualification.

title: Words as Infrastructure: Minority Languages, AI Governance and Linguistic Justice
journal: Strathprints: The University of Strathclyde institutional repository (University of Strathclyde)
abstract: Rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) are changing how people access information, communicate with institutions, and participate in public, educational, and cultural life. These benefits, however, are unevenly distributed across languages. English and a small number of other high-resource languages are well represented in AI systems, while many minority, minoritized, Indigenous and smaller state languages (referred to in this article as non-dominant languages) have a more limited digital presence. This conceptual article develops linguistic friction as a framework for analyzing the technical, linguistic, economic, and governance barriers that shape whether language communities can participate in, contribute to, and benefit from AI. Using an input–process–output framework, it examines how these barriers arise and interact across the AI lifecycle. It distinguishes linguistic friction from related concepts, including digital inequality, digital exclusion, linguistic injustice, and algorithmic bias, and argues that nominal language coverage does not guarantee functional equality. The analysis connects the material conditions of language technology with human rights, linguistic diversity and AI governance, identifying implications for digital infrastructure, community agency and accountability.
