title: Electromagnetic Braking System: Design, Working, and Applications
abstract: The advancement of modern transportation and machinery demands efficient, durable, and maintenance-free braking systems. Traditional friction brakes suffer from mechanical wear, noise, and heat generation. The electromagnetic braking system offers a promising alternative by utilizing magnetic forces to achieve smooth and contactless braking. This paper discusses the fundamental principles, working mechanism, design components, and comparative advantages of electromagnetic braking systems. A literature review has been included to analyze previous studies and advancements in this field. The applications, limitations, and future trends are discussed, highlighting the system’s potential to enhance safety, precision, and performance.

title: Torque-modulation-based train-borne measurement of the coefficient of friction at the wheel–rail interface
abstract: The Coefficient of Friction (CoF) at the wheel-rail interface critically influences train traction and braking performance, and thereby inter-train distance and track utilisation. Reliable measurement of the CoF experienced by in-service trains is therefore desirable to optimise railway operational schedules and maximise track capacity. This study presents a novel train-borne CoF measurement method based on a torque-modulation concept. The proposed method requires neither wheel sliding nor challenging train-borne creepage measurements, and does not rely on creep-force models, thereby addressing the limitations of current methods. A small-amplitude sinusoidal signal is superimposed on the motor torque. The wheel-rail friction force acts as variable damping, producing a phase difference between the input modulated torque and the angular speed response of the wheelset. This phase difference is correlated with the wheel-rail creep coefficient, i.e. the slope of the creep curve, and a threshold on the phase difference is determined to indicate the proximity of the operating point to friction saturation. As the torque is increased, the phase difference increases until this threshold is reached, and the corresponding CoF is output as the measurement. The method is evaluated in an ADAMS/VI-Rail-MATLAB/Simulink co-simulation environment, with results indicating accurate and robust performance across varied friction conditions.

title: Research on the Test and Evaluation of AEBS for Vehicles against Vulnerable Road User in Ice and Snow Environment
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: With the continuous advancement of vehicle safety technologies, the Automatic Emergency Braking (AEBS) system has become a key component in preventing traffic accidents. However, existing research and testing primarily focus on conventional road conditions, while the system’s performance under extreme environments such as snow and ice remains insufficiently investigated. This paper investigates the challenges encountered by AEBS when addressing Vulnerable Road Users (VRU) in low-friction snowy conditions, analyzing the degradation of sensor performance, uncertainties in decision-making, and actuator limitations arising from reduced friction and low-temperature effects. Furthermore, current regulatory frameworks lack comprehensive test scenarios for icy environments, with existing standards providing only limited assessments under static or simple motion conditions. To address these gaps, this study proposes six representative test scenarios defined by varying snowfall intensity levels, target object types, and vehicle motion states. The evaluation criteria focus on collision avoidance and vehicle stability after braking. The findings contribute to a more systematic and scientifically validated testing methodology for AEBS in winter environments, offering critical insights for future regulatory development and technological advancements in vehicle safety.

title: Interface Bonding and Geometric Effects on Microsurfacing Performance of Low-Volume Roads in the Peruvian Highlands
journal: Journal of Transportation Engineering Part B Pavements
abstract: Low-volume roads in mountainous regions often rely on economical pavement structures that are highly vulnerable to deterioration in horizontal curves. Conventional mechanistic–empirical design methods typically neglect horizontal forces, despite experimental and analytical evidence showing that lateral friction and braking significantly modify pavement response. This paper investigates the combined influence of horizontal curve geometry and interface bonding conditions on the structural performance of a microsurfacing over soil–cement base (MCP–BSC) pavement typical of low-volume roads in Peru. abstract: This chapter architectures the green mandate, reframing the climate crisis from an environmental ‘brake’ on development to the primary industrial engine of the Second Republic. title: Non-exhaust Emissions from the Tyre and Road Surface Interface – The Life-NEEVE State-of-the-art and Project Progress
abstract: Non-exhaust emissions (NEE) from the interaction between road surface and vehicle tyres are a growing, yet unregulated, source of particles contributing to air pollution in traffic environments. The source is complex and the factors affecting emissions and particle properties numerous. Abrasion of road surfaces depends on construction and material properties but also on tyres trafficking the surface. In countries where studded tyres are used, road surfaces abrade faster, and abrasion resistance is crucial. Tyre abrasion depends on tyre properties, road surface texture, vehicle properties (torque, weight) and driving behaviour. The emitted particles from tyre–road interaction are often heterogeneous aggregates where road surface wear particles are mixed into a tyre material matrix. Additionally, road dust is resuspended in tyre–road contact, a major air quality issue when road dust sources are strong and accumulation high. The Life-NEEVE project aims to reduce NEE by developing innovative road and brake materials and defining essential low-emitting tyre properties. This paper presents a road and tyre NEE state-of-the-art and ongoing Life-NEEVE progress.

abstract: Ethanol–gasoline blends are increasingly adopted to meet emission regulations and reduce dependence on fossil fuels; however, their application is constrained by low calorific value, high latent heat of vaporization, and poor cold‐start performance. title: Powertrain Systems Design for Heavy-Duty Trucks: Integrating Hybrid Electric Technologies with Low- and Zero-Carbon Fuel Engines to Reduce Fuel Consumption and Greenhouse Gas Emissions

abstract: Class 8 heavy-duty (HD) trucks are major contributors to global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, accounting for 50%, 40%, and 25% of transportation-sector emissions in the United States, Canada, and Europe, respectively. This thesis proposes new powertrain architectures and creates a vehicle-level design framework to evaluate the combined effect of hybridization and the use of natural gas (NG) or Hydrogen (H2) compression ignition (CI) engines on reducing fuel consumption and GHG emissions in Class 8 HD trucks. title: Toxicity-Weighted Assessment Reveals the Rising Dominance of Non-Exhaust PM2.5 from On-Road Transportation in China
abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) emitted from nonexhaust sources, here defined as brake and tire wear, is attracting attention as vehicle exhaust emissions decline due to advanced aftertreatment devices and rapid fleet electrification. However, the relative toxicity of nonexhaust PM2.5 compared with tailpipe emissions remains insufficiently quantified under a unified methodology. In this study, oxidative stress and cytotoxicity potencies of nonexhaust PM2.5 are 5- to 11-fold higher than those of exhaust PM2.5 via dynamometer tests, chemical analyses, and in vitro cellular assays. By integrating these toxic potencies with compiled emission inventories and modeling, toxicity-adjusted emissions of nonexhaust PM2.5 in 2023 expanded to nearly eight times those of exhaust PM2.5 in China. Exposure hotspots were disproportionately concentrated in economically developed regions with dense traffic. Projections forecast the nonexhaust proportion in toxicity-adjusted on-road emissions to surge from 54% in 2014 to an overwhelming 96% by 2050. While fleet electrification eliminates tailpipe exhaust and regenerative braking reduces brake wear, the nonexhaust PM2.5 proportion will keep rising in the absence of dedicated control measures. Our findings underscore an urgent imperative to incorporate nonexhaust sources into future air quality management, prioritizing eco-friendly material innovations and establishing standardized regulatory metrics to safeguard public health.

title: Influence of Fuel Injection Pressure on Gasoline/Waste Oil Biodiesel–diesel Blend (B20) RCCI Combustion: An Experimental Study
abstract: Waste oil-derived biodiesel is a promising renewable fuel for advanced combustion concepts such as Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI). However, the influence of fuel injection pressure (FIP) on gasoline/biodiesel RCCI combustion has received limited experimental attention. In this study, the effect of FIP was experimentally investigated using a diesel–waste cooking oil biodiesel blend (B20) as the high-reactivity fuel and gasoline as the low-reactivity fuel. Experiments were conducted at 1050 rpm with a premixed fuel ratio of 27%, over FIPs ranging from 150 to 350 bar and at two start-of-injection (SOI) timings of 25° and 40° bTDC. The study highlights that the response of different engine characteristics to variations in FIP depends on SOI for some parameters, whereas others are largely insensitive to SOI. Engine performance, combustion characteristics, and exhaust emissions were evaluated. The results showed that increasing FIP over a relatively large range increased brake power by up to approximately 2.4 times the minimum value, whereas the in-cylinder pressure peak did not follow the same trend. In addition, among the FIPs associated with relatively high brake power, an FIP was identified that resulted in lower NOx emissions at both SOIs while providing the highest brake power at one SOI. These findings demonstrate the importance of considering both FIP and SOI when selecting injection conditions for gasoline/B20 RCCI combustion.

In this article, aim is to investigate the extraction process of microalgae oil, its blending properties with diesel fuel, and evaluate its engine performance. The microalgae oil extracted through a solvent extraction method, and its physicochemical properties are analyzed. title: Environmental and energy performance assessment of a methanol–diesel RCCI engine through explainable machine learning
abstract: The transition toward sustainable transportation requires cleaner combustion technologies capable of improving efficiency while reducing environmental impacts. This study experimentally investigates the combustion, performance, and emission characteristics of a methanol–diesel Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) engine equipped with a Common Rail Direct Injection (CRDI) system. Methanol was supplied through port fuel injection to create a partially premixed charge, while diesel was directly injected as the high‐reactivity fuel. RCCI operation improved brake thermal efficiency to 29.8%, while reducing brake‐specific fuel consumption, CO, UHC, and smoke emissions; among tested conditions, the best performance was achieved at 23° BTDC and 500 bars. Net environmental benefit therefore depends on how this trade‐off is weighted, and on factors beyond the present scope such as after‐treatment and methanol production pathway. abstract: Even though hydrogen-augmented combustion may lead to high thermal loads and NOx emissions, both ethanol and hydrogen can reduce the spark ignition engine’s dependence on fossil carbon. abstract: The demand for carbon-free energy sources has increased the use of ethanol and hydrogen fuels in spark-ignition engines. The combustion process of these fuels relies heavily on the fuel injection and ignition techniques. In the present study, the effect of the combination of ethanol injection pressure and ignition timing (IT) on the performance of a hydrogen-assisted ethanol dual direct-injection engine is examined. A series of experiments were performed on a 0.5 L single-cylinder engine for ethanol injection pressures of 100 to 200 bar and ITs between 14° before top dead center (bTDC) and top dead center (TDC). abstract: This paper presents hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) utilize both high-voltage battery system and internal combustion engine to reduce fuel consumption and hazardous emissions. title: Machine Learning-Assisted performance prediction and analysis of Ammonia-Diesel Dual-Fuel engines
abstract: The brake thermal efficiency (BTE) and the NO X , NH 3 and N 2 O emissions of a 12.5 L marine low-pressure ammonia-diesel dual-fuel engine were predicted and analyzed using machine learning (ML). The dataset comprises 462 operating conditions accumulated during engine development with four hardware configurations, and it is unevenly distributed over the eleven input variables. Seven regression algorithms were compared by nested cross-validation with two data-splitting methods. With random splitting, the six nonlinear models did not differ significantly in mean R 2 (0.77 to 0.84). When similar operating conditions were excluded from the training folds, the tree ensembles retained the highest accuracy (mean R 2 of 0.67 to 0.71), whereas the neural network and Gaussian process models deteriorated considerably. None of the models could predict a hardware configuration that was absent from the training data. For the selected XGBoost model, the prediction error increased with the distance from the training data and with the disagreement among the seven models (Spearman ρ = 0.56). The distance did not explain the large errors at low load without the main diesel injection, where the combustion was less stable·NH 3 was the least accurately predicted output because of a few conditions with very high values. SHAP analysis showed that the air excess ratio (λ) was the most important input for NH 3 and N 2 O, and its opposite contributions to NO X and NH 3 agreed with the measured trends.

title: Sun-like stars show lowered X-ray activity together with over-rotation at beyond-solar ages
abstract: In recent years, substructure in the age-rotation relationship of cool, sun-like stars has been identified, showing deviations from the historical Skumanich law. Since magnetic activity is expected to be the physical root cause of the stellar spin-down, namely via the magnetic braking process mediated through stellar winds, changes in spin-down should correspond to unusual activity behaviour. We selected a sample of old sun-like stars in the solar neighborhood with asteroseismic age estimates and measured rotation periods, and present an analysis of their magnetic activity using deep X-ray observations from XMM-Newton. We observe that sample stars less massive than the Sun (late-G and early-K) agree well with the established rotation-activity relationship, while early-G and late-F stars with masses above solar tend to be unusually X-ray dim for their rotation period. The latter stars rotate faster than same-colour stars in the solar-age open cluster M67, despite being older than M67. title: Multi Response Optimization of Sustainable Hybrid Aluminum Matrix Composites Reinforced NPI Slag and Eggshell for Brake Disc Applications
abstract: This study aims to develop environmentally friendly Hybrid Aluminum Matrix Composites (HAMC) as an alternative material for brake discs using Nickel Pig Iron (NPI) slag and eggshells (ES). The composites were fabricated by stir casting using an Al 6061 matrix, with reinforcement compositions of NPI slag, ES, graphite, and Mg designed through a Taguchi L9 orthogonal array. Microstructural, density, porosity, tensile, and Brinell hardness evaluations were conducted, followed by multi-response optimization using the Data Envelopment Analysis-based Ranking (DEAR) method. Among the nine compositions, specimen S8 (3 wt.% NPI slag, 2 wt.% ES, 1 wt.% graphite, and 1 wt.% Mg) demonstrated the best overall performance, exhibiting relatively homogeneous particle distribution, the lowest porosity (1.5%), a tensile strength of approximately 200 MPa, and an elongation of 5.8%. Although S7 achieved the highest hardness (75 BHN), its tensile strength decreased to 115 MPa, primarily due to particle agglomeration. The DEAR analysis confirmed S8 as the highest-ranked experimental composition, with an MRPI of 1.599. Mg exhibited the greatest relative influence (Delta = 1.103), and the predicted optimum factor-level combination was NPI 2 -ES 2 -G 3 -Mg 1 . These findings highlight the importance of balanced reinforcement composition, particle distribution, and porosity control in optimizing HAMC performance.

abstract: The wheel hub connects the wheel and brake disc to the suspension of a vehicle. It is mounted on the wheel bearing, carries the wheel studs on its flange and transmits the weight of the vehicle, the cornering forces and the braking torque from the wheel to the knuckle. Because the hub rotates with the wheel, it is subjected to a load that changes direction once in every revolution, and a crack in its flange or spindle can cause the wheel to separate from the vehicle. The hub is also part of the unsprung and rotating mass, so a lighter hub improves ride, handling, acceleration and braking response. This paper presents the design and analysis of a front wheel hub for a compact passenger car with a gross mass of 1,250 kg. The hub, with a four-stud flange on a pitch circle diameter of 100 mm and an integral bearing seat, was modelled in CATIA and analysed in ANSYS Workbench. Four materials were compared on the same geometry, mesh and loads: grey cast iron, structural steel, aluminium alloy 6061-T6 and aluminium alloy 7075-T6. title: Microstructure–Tribology Relationship in Ti-6Al-4V Alloy After Short-Duration Low-Pressure Gas Nitriding
abstract: Ti-6Al-4V alloy is widely used in aerospace, biomedical, and engineering applications because of its high specific strength, corrosion resistance, and biocompatibility. However, its relatively low surface hardness and poor wear resistance limit its use under sliding-contact conditions. In this study, Ti-6Al-4V specimens were subjected to low-pressure gas nitriding at 950 °C for 60, 100, and 130 min to investigate the effects of short nitriding time on microstructure, hardness, and tribological behavior. The nitrided layers were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Cross-sectional microhardness, Rockwell C indentation, surface roughness, and dry sliding wear tests according to ASTM G99 were also evaluated. Low-pressure gas nitriding produced a graded surface region consisting mainly of a TiN/Ti2N compound layer and an α-Ti(N) diffusion zone. Increasing nitriding time promoted nitrogen penetration and development of the nitrided region. The N100 specimen exhibited the highest near-surface microhardness of approximately 550 HV0.025, whereas N130 showed a lower value of approximately 490 HV0.025. Despite its lower near-surface hardness than N100, N130 exhibited the lowest mean wear loss among the nitrided specimens, with a gravimetrically estimated wear volume of 0.722 ± 0.060 mm3 and a specific wear rate of (5.99 ± 0.50) × 10−4 mm3/(N·m).
